title: Paul Finebaum Blasts Commanders’ Jayden Daniels Over LSU Rift

Daniels wore No. 5 during his time with the Tigers and became the program’s third Heisman Trophy winner in 2023.As a result, Daniels’ attorney sent a cease-and-desist […] The post Paul Finebaum Blasts Commanders’ Jayden Daniels Over LSU Rift appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels is at odds with the LSU Tigers football program after the school gave his former No. 5 jersey to sophomore cornerback DJ Pickett. Daniels wore No. 5 during his time with the Tigers and became the program's third Heisman Trophy winner in 2023.

As a result, Daniels' attorney sent a cease-and-desist letter, a copy of which ESPN obtained, to LSU athletic director Verge Ausberry on Aug. 5, telling the school it could no longer use Daniels' name, image or likeness.

Amid the Commanders star's rift with LSU, Paul Finebaum of ESPN didn't hold back his thoughts on the situation and put Daniels on blast.

"I got to know Jayden Daniels when he was at LSU," Finebaum said during an Aug. 14 appearance on The Team 980. "I really liked him and talked to him a lot. I would interview Brian Kelly. Even when he went to the Commanders, there was a great sense of pride in what he did the first year.

"I said all that to say this: He's lost all of that from everywhere and everyone in LSU Nation after what happened this week [and] I know it's been said here before, but I rarely have ever seen a dumber, more senseless move.

"I don't know who pulled the strings, but all the cleanup on aisle three from Jayden Daniels from this moment on will not be enough. He has made a terrible mistake. He can be successful in Washington. I hope he is. But I would advise him to never waste another second in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, because they are done with him."

Moreover, Finebaum went into further detail on how the LSU crowd would receive the Commanders QB should he decide to head down to Baton Rouge to watch a Tigers game this 2026 college football season.

"I think it would be chillier than Inauguration Day at the nation's capital," Finebaum added about the reception that Daniels would receive from the crowd. "I think it's one thing if there was a misunderstanding, but when the report came out yesterday about the cease and desist and giving the trophy back, that's just pure stupidity.

"There are plenty of copies of the Heisman Trophy. I don't think anybody knows which one is the original because every school has one in its trophy case. Every player has one at home."

On Aug. 13, Joe Burrow, LSU's second Heisman Trophy winner, received a question after the Cincinnati Bengals' 16-14 preseason win over the Detroit Lions.

"I don't know too much about it," Burrow told reporters postgame. "I just heard about it a couple hours ago [and] I don't necessarily have too many thoughts at this time; I just don't know enough about the situation to have any thoughts, I would say."

Furthermore, Burrow spoke about whether LSU ever intends to hand out his No. 9 jersey, given that it is the issue Daniels is having with the football program.

"Like, they haven't," Burrow added. "Yeah, they told me that they wouldn't use it again, but you never know what happens."

title: 'Hey, buddy, I just crashed': Footage shows pilot walking away from fighter jet crash
description: The F/A-18 Hornet aircraft crashed in Washington in June.
fullText:
Dramatic new footage shows the moment local authorities encountered a pilot who had ejected from a fighter jet before it crashed into a mountainside in Washington state earlier this summer.

The F/A-18 Hornet aircraft slammed into a mountainside on June 13, in the area of Rimrock Lake, about 55 miles southeast of Seattle, sending a plume of black smoke into the air and igniting a wildfire.

The pilot assigned to Marine Aircraft Group 11, 3rd Marine Aircraft Wing, in Miramar, California, is seen with his face bloodied and appearing a little shaken up in the body camera footage released Friday by the Yakima County Sheriff's Office.

He is seen approaching deputies with his phone in his hand and 911 on the screen.

"What kind of jet is that?" the pilot is asked by one of the responders.

"That's an F-18," he replies. "Well, that was an F-18." He adds, "We were doing circles over the lake, doing some low-level training. ...And then I tucked in, and I'm not sure exactly."

"You hit the tree bad, bud," a witness states.

Later, the pilot is seen making a call to alert others to the wreck.

"Hey, buddy, I just crashed," the pilot says.

Later in the video, a parachute is seen hanging from a tree.

Responding officers with the sheriff's department said the pilot's injuries consisted of minor lacerations to his face.

In a news release at the time, the 3rd Marine Aircraft Wing said the pilot was conducting routine training when the aircraft experienced a "non-fatal aviation mishap."

The cause of the crash is still under investigation.

title: Commanders' Dorance Armstrong suspended for season opener vs. Eagles
description: Washington Commanders defensive end Dorance Armstrong receives a one-game suspension for violating the NFL's Personal Conduct Policy.
fullText:
Washington Commanders defensive end Dorance Armstrong has been suspended for the first game of the season for violating the NFL's Personal Conduct Policy. He will be eligible to participate in all preseason activities, including playing in Washington's preseason games.

His suspension begins on August 30, and he will be eligible for reinstatement on Mon. Sept. 14. This means he will miss Washington's season opener against the Philadelphia Eagles on Sun. Sept. 13. However, he will be available for the Commanders' game against the Dallas Cowboys on Sun. Sept. 20. Public records show that back in May of 2025, Armstrong was arrested in Frisco, Texas, for misdemeanor assault causing bodily injury as well as resisting arrest.

When Armstrong returns against the Cowboys in Week 2, it will be his first game since tearing his ACL against Dallas in Week 7 of last season. Prior to his torn ACL, Armstrong was having arguably the best season of his career with 5.5 sacks and seven tackles for loss in just seven games.

This year will be his third year with the Commanders and ninth season in the NFL. Armstrong spent the first six seasons of his career with Dallas, where he recorded a total of 23.5 sacks, 169 total tackles, and 48 quarterback hits. He has been a starter for most of his time with Washington and is expected to play a big role in the Commanders' defensive rotation this season.

fullText:
More students are advocating for their own digital wellbeing and developing programs to thrive in tech-free learning environments

As students across the country return to school this month, many will be confronting a new reality: classrooms without smartphones.

Educators and parents have long fronted the fight against the debilitating influence technology can wield. Yet, many young people say they have been left out of important conversations around school phone policies, which are now in effect in at least 39 states and Washington DC.

Student organizers told the Guardian they support screen-time bans in schools, but such policies are often haphazardly enforced and don’t address the root causes of screen addiction, such as intense social pressure and feelings of isolation. In response, more students are advocating for their own digital wellbeing and developing programs to thrive in tech-free learning environments.

Olivia Howard, a rising junior in New York state, recalled receiving her first iPad when she was in kindergarten. For digital natives like herself, she said, quitting their devices cold turkey was never going to be easy.

“We were the first generation to grow up on technology,” she said. “If legislators are implementing these phone bans, we need to take into account: what are the substitutes? Most kids my age have a relationship with technology, so there has to be other alternatives to replace it.”

In California, a new state law that took effect on 1 July requires school districts to develop policies that restrict phone use on campus. Elise Choi, a junior at the Orange County School of the Arts, said locking up devices is a step in the right direction but may not, on its own, be especially effective, since “kids will always find a way around regulations”.

As a K-12 policy co-chief with GENUp, a youth-led education advocacy group, Choi spent most of the year authoring and building a coalition for a state bill that would mandate district-wide digital wellness education, which teaches students how social media and AI affect their mental health.

“It’s not a matter of how long we’re on our devices but what it’s doing to us when we’re on it,” she said. “In general, the harm really extends beyond the classroom.”

Teens often stay up late scrolling on social media and texting, Choi said, which can cause insomnia and affect their ability to focus at school. Add to that the constant pressure to seek validation by garnering more “likes” or followers.

“Our entire social lives are happening online,” Choi said. “Digital wellness education is about giving students the understanding and skills to actually make better choices, set limits and understand the impact that it’s having on our health.”

Other students are proactively shaping phone bans at their schools. Liv Kong, a rising senior at Legacy Magnet Academy in Tustin, California, led a student advisory group that conducted surveys and rolled out three pilot phone policies to determine which one best suited students and faculty.

The idea for student-led pilots was formed a year ago, Kong said, after the school implemented a bell-to-bell ban without student input, which sparked a huge backlash. The students eventually chose a policy of banning phones in class but not during breaks.

“Growing up, I’ve seen that imbalance of power between the people who make decisions and the people those decisions affect,” Kong said. “Our mission was to make sure there’s student body representation in those decisions.”

Vihaan Bhardwaj, a rising senior at Mount Everest Academy and GENUp K-12 policy co-chief, said that when the San Diego school district banned phone use in classrooms last year, many students were apprehensive and confused about the intention behind the policy. In response, a committee with students from each school has been meeting regularly with top education officials to discuss how they can better communicate screen time mandates to students “in a way that feels supportive and not punitive”, he said.

“Young people are on the ground to make sure policies are implemented in the right ways,” Bhardwaj said. “As we’ve been able to talk to them, we’ve been able to make more students aware that these policies are there to help them, not to restrict their freedom or rights.”

Bhardwaj, 17, said he decided to join GenUP and the broader movement to ban phones from schools after an acne flare in middle school sent him spiraling.

“Social media made me feel like I was doing everything wrong – eating wrong, using the wrong products – making my experience with such a normal part of teenage life so dramatic, so life or death,” he said. “[It] took a lot of my energy.”

After New York enacted a statewide bell-to-bell anti-screen policy last year, the non-profit #HalfTheStory formed Teen Tech Council, a youth-led initiative that allows students to apply for mini-grants and launch tech-free initiatives on campus. Over the past year, the campaign has supported 50 schools and reached 17,000 students across the state.

Two teens in a rural school, noticing that phone use spiked after the art program was cut, placed rolling “crafts carts” around campus where students could use art supplies during and after school. At another school, a teen used the mini-grant to organize a phone-free scavenger hunt where students used disposable cameras to complete challenges.

Cayden Boahene, a recent graduate from Democracy Prep Endurance high school in the Bronx, used a portion of a $4,500 grant to host a Wellness Day event during finals week, where nearly 100 students shot hoops, played board games and formed new friendships without phones.

“I saw most of the students didn’t concentrate in class because of phones,” he said. “Some don’t connect with others and just connect through phones. I wanted to create an event to build real-world connections.”

Howard, who goes to Valley Stream North high school in Long Island, said social media fueled an urge to compare with others in a way that felt detrimental to her mental health.

“I thought everyone’s life was so perfect, so why is my life not like this?” she said, adding that the pressure intensified in high school as test scores and college prospects dominated conversations.

Since the phone ban went into effect, Howard said, the school had become livelier, with one professor observing that he had never heard so much noise and conversation in the hallways. But for more introverted students, she said, the suddenly raucous atmosphere was overwhelming. Instead of phones, some just turned to Chromebooks during lunch.

Over the past year, Howard and a group of students at Valley Stream have been working with school administrators to develop initiatives that would help students interact in a phone-free environment. This fall, she said, the school will be opening up a so-called “detox room”, furnished with books, stress toys and a sound machine, where students can “regulate their emotions” and relax.

Howard also urged teachers to create more opportunities for in-person connection in the classroom, including more group assignments.

“If someone’s super shy, that’s going to make them practice talking with other people,” she said.

fullText:
DUBAI, Aug 12 (Reuters) - There have been no talks on extending a ceasefire between Iran and the U.S. under an interim deal, with Iran saying that Washington ‌must return to the pact and define a timeframe to implement its commitments, a senior ‌Iranian source told Reuters on Wednesday.

The source's comments came after Turkey's Anadolu news agency, citing Pakistani government sources, reported that ​Tehran and Washington had agreed to extend a 60-day ceasefire under their Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).

"One of the issues that is being discussed via mediators is the U.S. returning to the interim agreement and defining a timeframe for implementing its commitments. There has been absolutely no progress on this issue," the source said.

The interim deal ‌signed in June between Tehran and ⁠Washington declared an "immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts", but quickly unravelled, with U.S. President Donald Trump saying on July 7 that the ⁠pact was "over". Tehran has repeatedly accused Washington of consistently violating its commitments.

"There is no talk of an extension because ... the United States violated the interim agreement 48 hours after it was reached and withdrew from it a ​few ​days later," the source told Reuters.

In the agreement, the ​60-day period refers to an extendable timeframe ‌within which Iran and the U.S. were expected to reach a final deal, which would include larger issues including the fate of Iran's disputed nuclear program.

A series of requirements, such as a ceasefire in Lebanon, free navigation in the Gulf and waivers for Iran to sell its oil, were viewed as necessary before entering the further negotiation period.

However, efforts to secure a lasting peace have hit an impasse over ‌a range of issues, including disagreements over the Strait ​of Hormuz.

Tehran says the vital shipping route will remain closed ​as long as the U.S. does not change ​its behaviour and accept Iran's conditions to end the war, including the unfreezing ‌of Iranian funds overseas.

After the start of ​the war, which began with ​U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, Tehran effectively shut the strait, through which a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas was shipped.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said ​on Sunday that Iran and the ‌U.S. are not engaged in talks and Tehran will not start them as long ​as Washington breaches the interim deal, adding that messages are being exchanged via intermediaries ​Pakistan and Qatar.

There is one more statistic that I did not mention before but would like to touch on here. Diggs ranked eighth in total receiving yards on motion plays last year. Keep in mind, he only played half of the Patriots total offensive snaps, so the number shows how effective he can be was when used in motion concepts. Not coincidentally, Blough is expected to incorporate them heavily in his new offense. As Blough stated earlier in the offseason:

I want it to be creative, aggressive, and I want whenever the coach on the other side turns the film on, I want them to feel stressed for every time we have the ball in our hands, of shifts, motions, breaking the huddle with urgency, getting us into premier plays."

This is how Diggs will alter Blough's offense. He won't change it conceptually but instead improve its effectiveness. Having another true threat opposite Terry McLaurin will allow Blough to stress the defense with motion and formation changes. If the veteran receivers line up on opposite sides, the defense must decide whether to shade safety help toward one boundary or the other. If Terry and Stefon align on the same side, Washington can stress and test communication through stacks and switch releases. Move either wide receiver into the slot; the defense has to reveal whether it will follow with a cornerback, pass the assignment to a nickel defender or change the coverage.

Washington can also use orbit or return motion to identify man coverage pre-snap. Forcing those decisions helps provide a clearer picture of the defense for quarterback Jayden Daniels before the snap and reduces the amount McLaurin needs to win in static alignments. Diggs represents that threat, and for those that have been following training camp, you can quickly see how Diggs differs from the players Washington already had in the wide receiver room.

Stefon Diggs looks GOOD!! That 18 ain’t bad either 👀#Commanders #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/skLLjntt66

Being "multiple" out of heavy personnel only works if the offensive play calling stays balanced out of these looks. The addition of Diggs will also allow the team to be effective with only two wide receivers. Along with Chig Okonkwo at tight end and a dual-threat running back, the defense must choose between a lighter coverage group or a heavier run-stopping option. If they go light, the offense can run the ball. If they go heavy, they can isolate a receiver against a linebacker or safety. Signing Diggs will allow Blough to keep both options credible and force the defense to honor them improving both the passing and rushing attack.

Just as importantly, Diggs gives Daniels another receiver he can trust, especially in hot reads and critical situations. Of Diggs' 85 catches last season, 51 of them resulted in first downs, for a 60% conversion rate. That falls in line with how Stefon has been for most of his career, as he has accounted for 561 first downs during his time in the league. Diggs also knows how to separate and win quickly, which has increased importance following the loss of Laremy Tunsil to a triceps injury.

Tunsil's absence will definitely be felt this season and may limit what Blough can do in multiple tight end sets and long-developing plays, but Adam Peters has already added another talent in Diggs that can elevate the Commanders offense and mitigate some of the loss this season.

title: Violent crime up in DC despite Trump boast of National Guard presence
description: Washington DC 2026 crime numbers show varying results from the National Guard deployment, which was ordered by President Donald Trump last year.
fullText:
President Donald Trump said during his State of the Union address in February that Washington DC has "almost no crime anymore" thanks to his deployment of the National Guard last August.

They were comments he took a step further in July, when he said DC has gone to levels of "NO CRIME" under his leadership.

The president is right; overall crime is down in DC. Fueled by a 53% drop in motor vehicle theft and a 37% decrease in theft from automobiles, there has been 23% less property crime in DC from 2026 to 2025, according to police data.

But numbers provided by the Metropolitan Police Department tell a different story, one that shows violent crime numbers are up this year.

Here's a look at the 2026 violent crime numbers in Washington DC and how they compare to 2025, with the National Guard deployment to continue through the entirety of Trump's presidency.

Trump's assertion that crime has been wiped out in DC falls short when compared to DC police statistics.

As of Aug. 10, there were 1,655 reported instances of violent crime in the city — 55 more than the same period from last year.

Most of that increase is due to a sharp upswing in reports of assault with a deadly weapon. There is a 41% increase in such activity, with 767 cases so far this year.

The data does show homicides are down — 67 cases this year, compared to 97 on this date in 2025 — but the summer has seen a dramatic increase.

There have been 32 homicides since the beginning of June, including nine in the past two weeks, police data shows.

While DC's homicide rates have improved, data shows that they're actually down throughout the country.

"It's really hard to parse out any effect of the federal deployment in DC, necessarily, because it is a city that was already seeing really strong declines," Jeff Asher, co-founder of the data analytics firm AH Datalytics, told USA TODAY earlier this year.

From 2024 to 2025 — less than half of which featured the National Guard's deployment — violent crime was down 29% in DC. There were 274 homicides in 2023 and 187 in 2024, and the city saw another decrease last year with 127 homicides.

title: A DC trial was nearing its end when the jury made a discovery that shocked everyone in the courtroom
description: The charges at a month-long criminal trial in Washington’s federal court last month were fairly straightforward: That one man had allegedly held up seven 7-Elevens and a few other gas stations in spri...
fullText:
The charges at a monthlong criminal trial in Washington's federal court last month were fairly straightforward: That one man had allegedly held up seven 7-Elevens and a few other gas stations in spring 2023 and stolen cars.

But the trial of Shamell Naquan Joyner had a twist. While deliberating, jurors found a Chinese yuan in one sweatshirt that was in evidence. And inside a jacket that was also part of the case, they found suspicious white powder in a folded up piece of paper. The prosecutors and judge said it appeared to be drugs.

The DC US Attorney's Office, law enforcement on the case and the defense team hadn't known.

The events of the jury deliberation raised eyebrows across the federal court in recent days, as word spread of what happened.

During deliberations, jurors are allowed to review evidence that is presented during the trial. Had the suspected drugs and yuan been part of the prosecution's case ahead of trial, it could have supported the case. But because it was a surprise, it could have been considered unfair to Joyner.

Several longtime lawyers in Washington told CNN last week they hadn't heard of a situation as embarrassing as this one, though some former prosecutors in DC conceded that every few years, a jury might land upon a piece of evidence that wasn't examined by law enforcement thoroughly enough.

Judge Rudolph Contreras, who presided over the trial, was flabbergasted.

"The Court shares Mr. Joyner's amazement at law enforcement's failure to uncover the Chinese Yuan, note, and powdery substance in the physical evidence," the judge, who has a decade of experience on the bench, wrote in an opinion a few days later.

"Mr. Liolos, who I know is from New York, is probably astonished that any money got past the police department," the judge also said on the bench, referring to John Liolos, one of Joyner's lawyers.

The FBI declined to comment when asked how agents on the case weren't aware of the drugs and money in the pockets.

When asked about how the evidence oversight happened, a spokesperson for the DC US Attorney's Office didn't answer directly.

Prosecutors alleged Joyner had robbed 10 convenience stores and gas stations in central Washington, Maryland and northern Virginia in the spring of 2023. The robberies at first started a few days apart in April, then by May 2, Joyner was hitting several in the same day, they alleged. He also was accused of armed carjackings around two of the days that the armed robberies occurred.

The series of incidents resulted in a 28-count indictment against Joyner in 2023. He wasn't charged with drug possession.

The case was big for the US Attorney's Office. The trial lasted a full month, with the jury hearing witnesses testify over 10 trial days, then deliberations lasting another week. Joyner had as many as nine lawyers and three prosecutors at trial.

As the jury was leaving on July 22, their second day of deliberations, a juror told courthouse staff they had found some items inside a jacket and a sweatshirt found in one of the carjacked cars that had been worn by the alleged robber.

"We were looking at (the jacket), and (one of the jurors) reached in the breast pocket and she pulled out — it looked like a receipt, but there was a white powder or white substance inside," the jury foreperson told the court on July 23, the next morning, according to a trial transcript obtained by CNN.

"Some of it, kind of, spilled out a little bit, but (a juror) put it back in the pocket and we put it back in the bag," the unnamed juror said.

There was a sweatshirt the jurors could examine too as evidence in the jury room. A juror had looked in the pocket there "and he pulled out — it was crumpled up — it was a bill … one of the Chinese Yuan bills," the foreperson then said.

When the jurors found the suspected drugs and money in the pockets at the end of the second day of jury deliberations, the issue opened up major legal questions for Joyner.

Both items of clothing had been key evidence putting Joyner at the scene of two of the May 2 robberies, and were inside the Toyota he was accused of stealing when police captured it a few days later.

Would the jurors be prejudiced against Joyner now? Had the jury finding the suspected drugs corroborated witness testimony from the trial further than what Joyner's defense lawyers anticipated?

The Justice Department argued that a witness testified about Joyner stealing money during the armed robbery of four different convenience stores. At one of the 7-Elevens, a witness said the robber took his wallet, and it had in it a Chinese Yuan from a college study abroad trip.

A cooperator who drove Joyner separately testified Joyner had paid him in drugs the night Joyner allegedly held up a gas station. The jacket with the apparent drugs in the pocket had been worn by the armed robber.

After the discovery in the pockets, Contreras brought each of the jurors into the courtroom one by one.

He told them the Chinese bill and the apparent drugs weren't part of the evidence in the case. The jurors each told the court they could set aside those items in their consideration of the case against Joyner.

They went back to deliberating.

The following Monday — the fifth day of deliberations — the jury had reached another predicament.

They said they realized they couldn't agree on more than half of the charges — representing five of the alleged armed robberies and one carjacking — Joyner faced.

"The jury remains deadlocked on or unable to vote on the remaining 15 counts in this case," they said in a note to the judge. "Our differences are in the areas of what constitutes a reasonable doubt and in how to determine identity beyond a reasonable doubt … In the absence of additional evidence or testimony, we cannot reach verdicts on the remaining 15 counts."

So, Contreras ended deliberations, taking a partial verdict.

The diligence of the jury, unable to come to an agreement on several of the charges against Joyner, echoed an unusual challenge the US Attorney's Office has faced in several other criminal trials this year.

Still, the jury found Joyner guilty of 13 criminal charges, representing an armed robbery in mid-April 2023 in downtown Washington, and four armed robberies and a carjacking on May 2, 2023, in Northwest Washington and Maryland.

"The jury's verdict ensures the defendant will face a 31year mandatory minimum sentence, making the D.C. community safer with this serial robber off the streets," a spokesperson from the US Attorney's Office said about the case.

Joyner's defense attorneys haven't yet appealed his conviction. They declined to comment because a final judgment in the case is not set in stone.

Correction: This story was updated to correct the year Joyner was indicted, which was 2023.

title: Phoenix Mercury’s road trip woes continue after loss to Washington Mystics
description: WASHINGTON — The Phoenix Mercury continued their tough road trip Sunday against the Washington Mystics, but had no answers as they fell 95-75, with their margin for error continuing to thin. Phoenix and Washington began the matchup competitively, both trading runs in the first quarter and separated by a single point.
fullText:
WASHINGTON — The Phoenix Mercury continued their tough road trip Sunday against the Washington Mystics, but had no answers as they fell 95-75, with their margin for error continuing to thin.

Phoenix and Washington began the matchup competitively, both trading runs in the first quarter and separated by a single point. However, that competitiveness vanished for the Mercury as the Mystics took charge the rest of the way with key shooting and tough defense that kept Phoenix from scoring more than 17 points in the second and third quarters.

Sixteen turnovers also turned into 18 points for Washington, highlighting Phoenix's inability to take care of the ball.

The Mercury's defense also had no answers for the Mystics' offense, allowing them to shoot 50% from the field and score 42 points in the paint.

Aug 9, 2026; Washington, District of Columbia, USA; Phoenix Mercury forward Valeriane Ayayi (11) drives past Washington Mystics guard Cotie McMahon (23) during the second half at CareFirst Arena. Mandatory Credit: Daniel Kucin Jr.-Imagn Images

What made the loss even more difficult was the early departure of Kelsey Plum, who left the game with left calf tightness. Plum was playing her fourth game with Phoenix since being acquired at the trade deadline, leaving the team without one of its dynamic shooters and playmakers.

Head coach Nate Tibbetts said the team wanted to play it safe, prioritizing Plum's health rather than pushing her.

The concern for Phoenix's playoff position is now more apparent than ever. With another three-game skid, the Mercury's chances for a postseason berth continue to slip away. The team's road trip has also made it difficult to find time to collect itself and practice, making it an even harder task for a group that has been trying to find consistency.

Aug 9, 2026; Washington, District of Columbia, USA; Washington Mystics center Shakira Austin (0) takes a shot during the first half against the Phoenix Mercury at CareFirst Arena. Mandatory Credit: Daniel Kucin Jr.-Imagn Images

"I think the biggest thing is just pride," Tibbetts said postgame when asked how to have his team reset without that practice time. "Just want to, competitive spirit and continuing to play."

While Sunday's loss came against one of the hottest teams in the WNBA, going toe-to-toe with Washington for one quarter showcased what Phoenix could have done if it had maintained its rhythm. However, when Washington punched back, the Mercury never found a way to recover.

Aug 9, 2026; Washington, District of Columbia, USA; Phoenix Mercury forward-guard DeWanna Bonner (24) dribbles the ball during the first half against the Washington Mystics at CareFirst Arena. Mandatory Credit: Daniel Kucin Jr.-Imagn Images

The Mercury will close out their five-game road trip in California when they take on the Los Angeles Sparks on Tuesday, Aug. 11, at 7 p.m.

title: Commanders lineman Sam Cosmi calls back Stefon Diggs joke in welcoming new teammate
description: Stefon Diggs signed on for a one-year deal with the Commanders on Wednesday, giving quarterback Jayden Daniels another solid weapon as Washington looks to return to the heights they reached in 2024. Offensive lineman Sam Cosmi decided to welcome his new teammate to the squad by bringing back an old joke that has followed Diggs…
fullText:
Stefon Diggs signed on for a one-year deal with the Commanders on Wednesday, giving quarterback Jayden Daniels another solid weapon as Washington looks to return to the heights they reached in 2024.

Offensive lineman Sam Cosmi decided to welcome his new teammate to the squad by bringing back an old joke that has followed Diggs since his time with the Vikings.

Asked for his first impressions of Diggs, Cosmi said, "He's a heck of a ballplayer. From a perspective of media, I wouldn't let him date my sister. I don't know where that came from in the locker room, so we'll see if that's a true thing."

Cosmi's comment calls back to a viral video that made Diggs infamous in his early seasons with the Vikings. Several players in the Minnesota locker room were asked which teammate they wouldn't want dating their sister, and Diggs was the immediate answer for many.

Sam Cosmi with a callback to this almost decade-old viral video when I asked him about Stefon Diggs
“I wouldn’t let him date my sister” https://t.co/NnK6my5bi4 pic.twitter.com/sdfkSuEFJU

— John Doran (@JohnDoranTV) August 7, 2026

Diggs had a good attitude about the initial video. "Nobody wants me to date their sister?" Diggs asked when he was informed that his name had been floated. "I'm a great guy! I'm actually a great guy. They just don't know me well enough."

At least Cosmi seems open to learning about his new teammate before making any final judgments. For the time being, the question might be mostly moot, as Diggs has a child with rapper Cardi B, and the two appear to have an on-again, off-again relationship of sorts. When Diggs was asked about their relationship status as of June, he responded, "You have to ask her."

title: Lakers urged not to sign $46M ex-Warriors NBA champion, focus on Klay Thompson, PJ Washington
description: The Los Angeles Lakers have been all in on a young NBA champion. However, it now seems like they are being told to move onto potential trades for either Klay Thompson or PJ Washington.
fullText:
Lakers urged not to sign $46M ex-Warriors NBA champion, focus on Klay Thompson, PJ Washington originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Los Angeles Lakers have been all-in on Jonathan Kuminga since LeBron James informed the team that he would no longer be returning. However, it has been a lengthy process for Los Angeles to get a deal done.

Even throughout this process, the Lakers have not wavered and remain focused on Kuminga. Landing a deal for the young forward remains LA's top priority as the offseason continues.

"Jonathan Kuminga remains the Lakers' top free agent target before finishing their offseason. As the Cavaliers have pivoted to chasing Peyton Watson, Kuminga is the sole focus currently for Los Angeles. There could soon be momentum gathering on Kuminga to LA via sign-and-trade," NBA reporter Evan Sidery wrote.

With the Lakers seemingly being Kuminga's preferred destination, it still appears that his camp and the Atlanta Hawks are creating obstacles to a potential sign-and-trade. Nothing has moved in weeks, largely because Atlanta has not been satisfied with the trade package it could receive in return.

"It has reached the second month of what has become a second consecutive prolonged Kuminga free agency process. The Lakers met with Kuminga in the early hours of free agency, pitching him on a high-minutes role for a high-profile fringe contender in desperate need of athletic help on the wing. The opportunity appealed to Kuminga, but the sign-and-trade contract offer (years, money, package going back to Atlanta) didn't satisfy all sides. The Lakers remain interested in him, league sources said, but movement toward a deal has remained stalled for weeks," ESPN's Anthony Slater wrote.

With the process continuing to drag on, the Lakers have now been urged to move on from Kuminga and prioritize a trade for either Klay Thompson or P.J. Washington.

"Obviously, anything can change during the NBA offseason, as Kuminga could have a change of heart or decide Los Angeles is the best situation for him, but it seems like it is time for the storied franchise to move on. Perhaps the Lakers should focus on trading for Klay Thompson or P.J. Washington, both of whom have experience playing with Doncic," SI's Ryan Ward wrote.

At this point, it is fair to say that moving on from Kuminga would not necessarily be a bad idea. The Lakers have been pursuing him for nearly two months, and nothing has been finalized.

Kuminga was on a $46 million contract last season, while the Lakers are looking for someone who can make an immediate impact. It remains unclear whether Kuminga would be able to do that right away, but Thompson and Washington have already proven themselves throughout their careers.

For the Lakers, the decision ultimately comes down to how long they are willing to wait for Kuminga versus how quickly they can find another option to strengthen the roster around Luka Doncic.
